# Draft:Battle of Ewulu

The Battle of Ewulu (also spelt Ehulu, Hulu or Leolu)  was a Swazi-Sotho War fought in 1869 in the north-eastern Transvaal region. The battle began when  Swazi forces attempted to support the restoration of disputed Bapedi heir Prince Mampuru II against his half-brother King Sekhukhune, ending in a devastating defeat for the Swazi.
It was fought at the Leolo Mountains (Ehulu/Ewulu) in the north-eastern Transvaal region in modern-day west of Mpumalanga and south-eastern Limpopo provinces in Sekhukhuneland.
Background
Under King Mswati II, Swazi regiments advanced westward into the Steelpoort and Lydenburg area, defeating several communities, particularly  Sotho and Mambayi speaking communities and consolidating Swazi power.
By 1866, King Mswati II's forces had already carried out major raids across the Lowveld, crossing the Great Letaba River and attacking several communities, including the Lobedu under Queen Modjadji and other groups along the escarpment such as the Nkuna under Chief  Shiluvane.
Following the king’s death in 1868, the Kingdom began the 3-year mourning period. While the Kingdom was in mourning, several Swazi war leaders, like Matsafeni Mdluli, proposed launching a ritual military expedition intended to “cleanse the spears” after the death of the monarch.
Such expeditions were traditionally undertaken against rival groups, and in this case the proposed target was the Bapedi.
However, the Queen mother, Tsandzile Ndwandwe, opposed the proposal and said a nation could not go to war without a king.
According to Swazi custom, when a military expedition was undertaken the reigning king was expected to perform ritual observances while fasting at the royal residence to ensure the army’s success.
Because the king had died and a successor had not yet fully assumed power, the queen regent argued that the necessary rituals could not properly be performed.
While on that issue, the disputed Bapedi heir Prince Mampuru II, exiled in Swaziland, was looking for Swazi support to dethrone his half-brother King Sekhukhune whom he accused of being illegitimate.
Acting without the approval of the queen regent, Matsafeni proceeded with the expedition to help restore Prince Mampuru II and led Swazi regiments into the mountainous area of Leolo/Ewulu in Sekhukhuneland.
After reaching the Leolo/Ewulu Mountains, the Swazi forces were drawn into a trap in a mountainous area where Bapedi forces had taken distant positions on surrounding hills. When the Swazi army was fully exposed, rifle fire was opened on them from multiple directions. The Swazi, who were primarily armed with spears and traditional weapons, suffered heavy losses.
Many warriors, including members of the royal house, were killed. One of the royal members killed at the battle was Prince Msukusuku, a son of King Sobhuza I with Queen Mnyezane Zulu. After the battle, one warrior, Mhlaphahlapha Maseko, saw the badly injured and dying Msukusuku. He asked Mhlaphahlapha to finish him off to save him from his pain and Mhlaphahlapha stabbed him, and brought his weapons home.
Disgraced, Matsafeni disappeared for six months without trace and on return was blamed by the royal family for the war.
The defeat confirmed the authority of Sekhukhune and marked a significant setback for Swazi military ambitions in the region.
Mampuru remained exiled in Swaziland until later restored to the Pedi throne in 1879 with the support of British and  Swazi forces.
